n: “But now” — Job’s present stands in shocking contrast to his past. Young men from the lowest class mock him, though Job wouldn’t have trusted their fathers to watch his sheepdogs.

f.g: Laugh at me, mock me.
Sheepdogs — low-status working animals.

n: Their strength was useless to him; they were worn-out men with no vigor left.

f.w: in whom old age was perished
f.g: Men whose strength had wasted away.

n: Starving and desperate, they gnawed the dry ground of the desert wasteland at night.

f.g: Gaunt, barren.

n: They picked salty desert plants and broom-tree roots for food — the food of outcasts.

f.g: Probably saltwort, a bitter desert plant.
The broom tree, a desert shrub.

n: They had been driven out of society, shouted at as if they were thieves.

f.w: they cried after them as after a thief
f.g: People raised an alarm against them.

n: They had to live in gullies, caves, and among the rocks.

f.g: Clefts, ravines.

n: They brayed like animals among the bushes and huddled under the thorns.

f.g: Weeds or thorny scrub.

n: They were nameless outcasts, a senseless and disreputable crowd driven from the land.

f.g: Literally “sons of no name” — people of no standing.

n: And now these very outcasts make up songs mocking Job; he has become their joke.

f.g: An object of ridicule.

n: They despise him, keep their distance, and don’t hesitate to spit in his face. Many see in this a foreshadowing of how Christ was treated.
Because God has unstrung Job’s bow and humbled him, they throw off all restraint toward him.

f.g: Unstrung my bow — taken away my strength.
Cast off all restraint.

n: A mob rises at his right side, pushes him off his feet, and builds siege ramps against him.

f.g: Siege ramps — military imagery.

n: They break up his path and promote his ruin, and no one restrains them.

f.g: Break up, ruin.

n: They pour in like soldiers through a wide gap in a wall, rolling over him amid the ruins.

f.w: a wide breaking in of waters
f.g: A wide breach in a city wall.

n: Terrors overwhelm him; his dignity is blown away like wind and his safety drifts off like a cloud.

f.w: my welfare passeth away as a cloud

n: His life is ebbing away, and days of suffering grip him.
At night pain pierces his bones, and the gnawing never stops.

f.g: Literally “my gnawers do not rest” — constant, gnawing pain.

n: His disease is so severe it disfigures his clothing, which clings to him like a tight collar.

f.w: bindeth me about as the collar of my coat
f.g: His skin or garment chokes him like a tight neckband.

n: God has thrown him into the mud; Job feels he has become no more than dust and ashes.
Job turns to God directly: I cry to you and you don’t answer; I stand before you and you only stare.
Job feels God has become cruel and attacks him with a mighty hand. This is Job’s honest feeling, not the book’s final word about God.

f.w: Thou art become cruel to me

n: He feels lifted into a storm wind, tossed about, and dissolved in its roar.

f.g: Toss me about in the storm until I melt away.

n: Job expects God to bring him to death, the house appointed for everyone who lives.

f.w: the house appointed for all living
f.g: The grave, which awaits all.

n: Surely no one would strike a ruined person who reaches out a hand and cries for help in disaster.

f.w: he will not stretch out his hand
f.g: The Hebrew is difficult; Job seems to ask why a fallen man is not given mercy.

n: Job reminds God that he himself wept for people in trouble and grieved for the poor.

f.w: Did not I weep for him that was in trouble?

n: He expected good, but evil came; he hoped for light, but darkness fell.

f.w: when I waited for light, there came darkness

n: His insides churn without rest; days of affliction confront him.

f.g: The inner parts — seat of deep feeling.
Came to meet, confronted (old sense of “prevent”).

n: He walks about darkened (by grief or disease) without sunlight, and stands up in the assembly crying for help.

f.g: Blackened, in gloom — perhaps also his darkened skin.

n: He has become a brother to jackals and a companion of ostriches — desert creatures known for mournful cries.

f.g: Jackals.
Ostriches.

n: His skin turns black and peels, and his body burns with fever.

f.w: my bones are burned with heat

n: His lyre plays only funeral songs, and his flute only the sound of weeping. All his joy has turned to mourning.

f.w: My harp also is turned to mourning

f.g: A flute or pipe.
